headline: Passkey verification moves onto the PKI toolkit the framework already ships, the `@simplewebauthn/server` bundle is gone, and the ceremony now refuses cross-origin registrations and logins
summary:
`b.auth.passkey` verified WebAuthn attestations and assertions through a second vendored library. `@blamejs/pki` — already in the tarball for `b.mtlsCa` — does the same job, so the 889 KB `@simplewebauthn/server` bundle no longer ships. One fewer third-party bundle to track advisories against, and no new dependency to replace it.

The surface is deliberately unchanged: the same four calls, the same options, the same result fields, and the same stored-credential bytes, so existing credential rows keep working and no migration is needed.

What is new is a check the previous verifier never made. `CollectedClientData.crossOrigin` says whether the ceremony ran inside an iframe rather than at the top level, and nothing read it — a registration or login driven from a hostile embedding page was indistinguishable from one the user performed on your site, because the signature, challenge, origin and RP ID all genuinely check out. Both ceremonies now refuse it.

One behaviour narrows in a way that can need action: the verifier accepts the three algorithms the framework advertises, where the previous one advertised three and accepted ten. If your deployment issued credentials outside that set, name them in `allowedAlgorithms` — details below.

items.title: Cross-origin ceremonies are refused by default
items.body:
`CollectedClientData` carries a `crossOrigin` flag, set by the browser when WebAuthn ran in a frame whose top-level origin is not yours. The previous verifier never read it.

That leaves an embedded ceremony looking exactly like a legitimate one: the credential really was used at your origin — inside somebody else's page, driven by their script, at a moment the user did not choose. The user sees their own authenticator prompt and approves it.

`verifyRegistration` and `verifyAuthentication` now refuse `crossOrigin: true` with `auth-passkey/cross-origin-ceremony`.

A deployment that genuinely is embedded — a checkout widget, a partner portal — names the embedders it has:

```js
allowCrossOrigin: ["https://partner.example"]   // matched against clientData.topOrigin
```

`allowCrossOrigin: true` accepts any embedder, for the case where the partner set is not a list you can write down. A browser that reports `crossOrigin` without naming the top origin never satisfies a list — an unnamed embedder is the case the list exists to exclude.

items.title: Manufacturer attestations are anchored to pinned vendor roots
items.body:
An `apple` or `android-key` attestation statement proves which authenticator model created a credential — which is the entire reason to ask for `attestation: "direct"`. That proof is only worth its anchor: checking the statement's signature and certificate profile without checking WHERE the chain terminates accepts a manufacturer claim rooted in a CA the attacker created.

The six vendor roots (Apple's WebAuthn root, Google's four hardware-attestation roots, and the GlobalSign root the SafetyNet JWS chains to) are pinned in the framework and handed to the verifier, rather than read from the host trust store — the store is operator-mutable and carries hundreds of unrelated roots, any one of which could otherwise mint an "Apple" authenticator. `android-safetynet` registrations are verified again rather than refused as an unsupported format, and with the two checks that make one worth having: Google's `ctsProfileMatch` must be true (a correctly-signed statement that the device FAILED compatibility testing is still a failure), and the response must be less than 60 seconds old and not dated in the future. A device-integrity claim is about a moment; without an age bound, one captured response replays for as long as the challenge stays outstanding. `requireCtsProfileMatch: false` and `safetyNetMaxAgeMs` move those.

Anchors are chosen per format: `apple` chains to Apple's root, `android-key` to Google's, `android-safetynet` to GlobalSign. A `compound` statement (WebAuthn 8.9) nests several attestations, each with its own trust path, and is refused rather than anchored off its outer format alone — which would leave a nested manufacturer element unanchored. The verifier this replaces did not implement `compound` either, so nothing that worked before stops working. `packed`, `tpm` and `fido-u2f` are deliberately not anchored against this bundle — those chains end at whichever vendor made the key, so there is no fixed set to pin, and WebAuthn anchors them through the FIDO metadata entry for the credential's AAGUID instead (`b.auth.fidoMds3`). `none` and self attestation carry no chain at all and are unaffected.

A deployment that trusts a different set passes `attestationRoots` (and `safetyNetRoots`), which REPLACE the format's pinned set rather than extending it — naming your own anchors is narrowing trust, and quietly adding the vendor roots back would defeat that. An empty or malformed override is refused rather than falling back to the default.

items.title: Binary response fields must be canonical base64url
items.body:
`authenticatorData`, `signature`, `clientDataJSON` and `attestationObject` are now required to be canonical base64url. Node's decoder discards characters it does not recognise, so `AQ!ID` and `A Q I D` decode to the same bytes as `AQID` — the verifier saw the genuine signed bytes and returned `verified: true` while the response as posted had unboundedly many spellings.

That matters beyond tidiness: anything keyed on the response as sent — a replay cache, an idempotency key, a request digest — counts each spelling as a new request.

items.title: A response must state the one credential type WebAuthn defines
items.body:
WebAuthn has exactly one credential type, `"public-key"`. A registration or assertion whose outer `type` is missing or altered is now refused with `auth-passkey/bad-credential-type`, rather than the value being defaulted into `registrationInfo.credentialType`.

Writing a type nothing verified into a credential row misleads anything that later dispatches on it, and storing the attacker's string does so more directly.

items.title: Both spellings of the credential ID are bound to the credential being used
items.body:
A WebAuthn response states its credential ID twice — `id` and its binary spelling `rawId` — and neither is covered by any signature. Registration checks both against the ID inside the attestation, which the authenticator signs; authentication checks both against the stored record.

This is not what admits an attacker — a mismatched record carries the wrong public key, so the signature fails regardless. It is about what an operator is told when it happens. An application that looks a credential up by user rather than by asserted ID could pair a valid key with the wrong row and see only an opaque signature failure; it now gets `auth-passkey/credential-id-mismatch`, which names the actual problem.

items.title: The FIDO metadata trust root is pinned in the source
items.body:
`b.auth.fidoMds3` anchored MDS3 BLOB chains to a GlobalSign Root CA - R3 certificate read out of the removed bundle. That certificate is now a constant in the framework, and a test asserts its subject, self-signature, validity window and SHA-256 fingerprint — so substituting it during a refactor fails a gate instead of silently widening what can sign a metadata BLOB.

The `caCertificate` override is unchanged, and still replaces the pinned root rather than adding to it.

items.title: Verified algorithms are the advertised ones — widen with `allowedAlgorithms` if you issued others
items.body:
`startRegistration` has always offered Ed25519, ES256 and RS256. The verifier behind it accepted ten algorithms, including RSA with SHA-1. It now accepts exactly what is offered.

An authenticator is supposed to pick from the advertised list, so for most deployments nothing changes. But the wider set was accepted for as long as it was offered, so a credential registered outside it may exist — and refusing its assertions locks that user out of an account they can still prove they own.

`allowedAlgorithms` names the set for a call, and drives both halves of a ceremony: what `startRegistration` offers and what the verifiers enforce, so a deployment cannot advertise one set and accept another.

```js
await b.auth.passkey.verifyAuthentication({
  response, expectedChallenge, expectedOrigin, expectedRPID, credential,
  allowedAlgorithms: [-8, -7, -257, -36],   // + ES512, for credentials issued earlier
});
```

Supported identifiers are -8, -7, -35, -36, -37, -38, -39, -257, -258, -259 — every one of them exercised end to end, so the list cannot advertise an algorithm the verifier would then refuse. The default is unchanged and the option applies only to the call it is passed to. RSA with SHA-1 (-65535) is refused however it is asked for: the option exists to keep working credentials working, not to make a broken primitive reachable through configuration, and a credential using it has to be re-registered. An unsupported identifier, a non-integer, or an empty list is refused at the call rather than falling back to the default.

If you are unsure which algorithms your table holds, the COSE key's `alg` (label 3) in each stored `credential.publicKey` is the answer.

items.title: `@simplewebauthn/server` is no longer vendored
items.body:
Attestation and assertion verification, CBOR parsing, COSE key handling and signature checking now run in `@blamejs/pki`, which the framework already vendors. Nothing about `b.auth.passkey`'s API changes: the same calls, options, result fields, and stored-credential format — the persisted public key is the authenticator's COSE key bytes verbatim, as before.

The ceremony options `startRegistration` and `startAuthentication` return are now built in the framework rather than delegated. They are plain JSON documents the browser reads, with no secret in them beyond the challenge, and the challenge comes from `b.crypto.generateBytes` like every other secret the framework mints.

`registrationInfo.credential.publicKey` is now a `Buffer` rather than a bare `Uint8Array`. A `Buffer` is a `Uint8Array`, the bytes are identical, and code that stores or compares it is unaffected.

items.title: A credential key stored as base64url text is read as base64url
items.body:
`credential.publicKey` may now be handed back as a `Buffer`, a `Uint8Array`, or the base64url string an operator wrote to a TEXT column. Previously a string was neither decoded nor rejected — it was read as UTF-8, producing bytes that are not a COSE key, and the login failed with a message about a malformed credential while the stored row was perfectly intact.

A string that is not canonical base64url, and any other type, is now refused as `auth-passkey/bad-credential-key` rather than coerced into bytes that merely happen to parse. Correct `=` padding is accepted and matters here more than anywhere: a COSE key's length usually calls for it — an ES256 key is 77 bytes, 103 characters plus one `=`.

items.title: A bad attestation signature is a negative result, not an exception
items.body:
A registration whose attestation signature does not verify is the registration-side equivalent of a failed login — an ordinary negative outcome. It was being raised as an `AuthError`, so a caller writing `if (!result.verified) deny()` took an exception path and returned a 500 where a refusal belonged.

It now returns `{ verified: false, registrationInfo: null }`, matching both the authentication path and the verifier this release replaced. Everything else — a binding that disagrees, an unanchored chain, a policy the ceremony failed — still throws, because which check refused is the actionable part.

`apple`, `tpm` and `android-key` are the exception and keep throwing. Those formats report a failed attestation *binding* — the Apple nonce, TPM's `certInfo` extraData and attested Name, Android Key's KeyDescription (`attestationChallenge`, `allApplications`, key origin and purpose) — through the same underlying code as a bad signature, and a binding violation is an attack indicator rather than an ordinary decline. The negative result is an allow-list of the formats where that code means a signature and nothing else, so a format it does not recognise keeps the exceptional path.

items.title: `residentKey` and `requireResidentKey` can no longer disagree
items.body:
WebAuthn states "this credential must be discoverable" in two places: `residentKey`, and the Level 1 boolean `requireResidentKey`. Browsers in the field read one or the other, so the pair has to agree.

`startRegistration` read the caller's two inputs independently, which let them contradict: `{ residentKey: "required" }` emitted `requireResidentKey: false`, and the legacy boolean on its own was dropped entirely — `{ requireResidentKey: true }` emitted `residentKey: "preferred"`.

A browser honouring the half that says "not required" then creates a non-discoverable credential for a relying party that required a discoverable one. Nothing fails at registration; the credential works, and only username-less and conditional-UI login are quietly missing.

Both fields now come from one resolved requirement. `residentKey` decides when present, the legacy boolean still states the requirement on its own, and `requireResidentKey` always equals `residentKey === "required"`.

items.title: Default authenticator hints follow `authenticatorAttachment`
items.body:
`hints` and `authenticatorAttachment` both say which authenticator a ceremony is for, and the browser gives hints precedence in the UI. The default hint list did not consider the attachment, so a ceremony restricted to `cross-platform` still hinted at the platform authenticator — offering the user a path the attachment forbids, and refusing the credential on the one they picked.

With no explicit `hints`, the default is now `["security-key", "hybrid"]` for `cross-platform` and `["client-device"]` for `platform`. With no attachment set it is unchanged. An explicit `hints` list still passes through untouched.

items.title: A multi-origin deployment records which origin the ceremony ran at
items.body:
`expectedOrigin` accepts an allow-list, for one relying party served from several origins. Both verification results reported that list back as the ceremony's `origin` — so a field every consumer reads as a string held an array, and an audit row named every permitted origin instead of the one that was actually used.

Both results now carry the origin from the verified client data. A single-origin deployment sees no change.

items.title: `credProps`, `transports`, signed extension outputs and padded credential IDs all survive the move
items.body:
Four things the previous verifier did that the move had dropped.

`credProps` is requested on every registration again, and the browser's answer now reaches the result. `residentKey: "preferred"` lets the authenticator decline, so without asking, an application cannot tell which of its credentials support username-less or conditional login — it has to assume the worse case for all of them. The request is merged over whatever extensions the caller asked for, and `registrationInfo.clientExtensionResults.credProps.rk` carries the reply.

That field is kept separate from `authenticatorExtensionResults`, and the distinction matters: client extension results are reported by the browser and nothing signs them, while authenticator extension results sit inside the bytes the attestation signature covers. `credProps.rk` is a UX signal, not a guarantee to gate on.

`registrationInfo.credential.transports` carries the browser's `getTransports()` through again. Persist it, hand it back in `allowCredentials`, and the next login goes straight to the right transport instead of prompting for all of them.

`authenticatorExtensionResults` is back on both results, decoded from the signed authenticator data through `b.cbor`. These are the authenticator's own `credProtect` / `credBlob` answers — inside the bytes the signature covers, unlike `clientExtensionResults`, which the browser reports and nothing signs. Nested structures (`largeBlob`, `devicePubKey`) are converted all the way down: a CBOR map left in place looks right in memory and serializes to `{}`, so persisting or logging the result would drop verified data with nothing failing. Integer CBOR labels are kept as their decimal string form, so a nested COSE key — `devicePubKey`'s `dpk` is labelled entirely with integers — arrives with its entries rather than as an empty object. The converted object has a null prototype, so an extension legitimately named `__proto__` stays an own property instead of hitting the prototype setter and disappearing from `Object.keys()` and JSON.

The authentication result's `userVerified`, `credentialDeviceType`, `credentialBackedUp` and backup flags are read from the bytes the verifier checked rather than re-read from the response afterwards. Verification is asynchronous and the caller holds that object throughout, so a second read could report flag bits no signature covered.

A credential ID carrying `=` padding is accepted and normalized rather than refused. base64url is canonically unpadded, but plenty of encoders emit it, and a stored credential ID is whatever the encoder of the day wrote. Refusing it rejected no attack — it stopped affected deployments from starting authentication at all. The credential-ID binding compares canonical forms for the same reason, so a padded stored ID and the unpadded spelling the browser returns are one credential rather than a mismatch.

IDs that do not canonically name one credential are still refused: Node's base64 decoder is lenient in ways that silently produce a DIFFERENT id — `YW` re-encodes to `YQ`, and a lone leftover character decodes to nothing — so an id is accepted only if re-encoding the bytes it decodes to reproduces it.

The same rule now covers the Signal API builders (`signalUnknownCredential`, `signalAllAcceptedCredentials`, `signalCurrentUserDetails`), where it matters more than anywhere else: the browser acts on those identifiers. `signalUnknownCredential` asks it to remove the named credential, and `signalAllAcceptedCredentials` is exhaustive — the browser deletes passkeys absent from the list. An id that decodes to different bytes removes the wrong passkey, or leaves the right one off the list and has the browser delete it. They also normalize correctly-padded ids rather than refusing them.

items.title: Every passkey refusal is an `AuthError`, framed exactly once
items.body:
A stale or replayed registration challenge — the most ordinary failure a WebAuthn deployment sees — escaped as the verification library's own error type with a `webauthn/*` code. The documented contract is `catch (e) { if (e.isAuthError) ... }` with an `auth-passkey/*` code, the same framing as `b.auth.password` and `b.auth.totp`, so that handler missed it and the request became a 500.

Every call into the verifier is now re-framed through one path, and which check refused is still carried in the code. That path leaves an error this module already raised alone: a missing binary field or an undecodable stored key produced `auth-passkey/auth-passkey/bad-response`, a code matching nothing a caller dispatches on.

items.title: `passkey-credential-id-binding-goes-through-the-helper`
items.body: A hand-rolled comparison of `response.id` or `response.rawId` in the passkey module fails the pattern gate. A response states the same identity in two spellings; binding one and forgetting the other is how the two ceremonies would come to enforce different rules, so the check lives in one helper that takes both.

items.title: `passkey-result-origin-is-the-verified-one-not-the-allowlist`
items.body: `origin: opts.expectedOrigin` in either ceremony's result fails the pattern gate. The option may be an allow-list; the result field is a single verified origin, and the two ceremonies reached for the wrong one independently.

items.title: `passkey-resident-key-selectors-derive-from-one-requirement`
items.body: Reading the caller's `requireResidentKey` alongside `residentKey` fails the pattern gate. One requirement stated in two fields has to be resolved once and written twice, not read twice.
